articles.title: THE MACHHOLTZ MARATHON
articles.summary: Don Machholtz delivered a highly praised talk at a March SJAA meeting, detailing the Messier Marathon, including execution, historical context, and expectations. He noted that completing the marathon in a single night necessitates traveling south of the Bay Area, though a quarter moon or less would not pose a significant problem. The presentation was lauded for its informational content, wit, and anecdotes, despite Machholtz being unwell.

articles.title: MAY
articles.summary: This document outlines a calendar of astronomical events and activities for May and June, primarily hosted by an astronomy club. It includes multiple star parties at Houge Park and Fremont Peak, general meetings with speakers like John Dobson, and various astronomy classes. Key events also include Astronomy Day, the Riverside Telescope Maker's Conference, and a weekend trip to Yosemite National Park.

articles.title: MESSIER MARATHON REPORT
articles.summary: Jay Freeman reports on his solo attempt at a Messier Marathon on March 28, 1998, in the southern San Francisco Bay Area. Despite prior planning among local amateur astronomers, he found himself alone at both designated observing sites, Fremont Peak and Henry Coe State Park. Challenging weather, including thunderstorms and poor seeing, affected his observing conditions and limited his ability to fully set up his new Meade 127 ED refractor.

articles.title: Messier, from p. 1
articles.summary: An astronomer successfully observed 40 Messier objects and several NGC galaxies in under an hour, despite rough equipment alignment and less-than-perfect sky conditions. Notable observations included details in M97 and the Sombrero, and resolved clusters M44, M67, and M40. The session concluded early due to distant lightning and encroaching clouds, though rain did not immediately follow.

articles.title: DOBSON AT SJAA MEETING
articles.summary: John Dobson is scheduled to speak at the San Jose Astronomical Association's (SJAA) May 9 General Meeting. The article encourages attendance to learn about his significant contributions to amateur astronomy, promising an entertaining, witty, and informative evening. Dobson previously made a cameo appearance at the March meeting where Don Machholtz gave a talk.

articles.title: Akkana Peck
articles.summary: May offers early morning observing opportunities for several planets, including Uranus, Neptune, Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, and Saturn. Notable events include Mercury and Saturn's close pass on May 13, and Venus and Jupiter's close pass on May 29, with Pluto reaching opposition on May 28. The primary meteor shower for the month is the Eta Aquarids, peaking on May 5, known for producing frequent trains.

articles.title: Ernie Piini
articles.summary: The article recounts Ernie Piini's successful observation of the February 26, 1998 total solar eclipse from a church site in the Caribbean. Despite sacrificing a few seconds of totality for wind protection and avoiding crowds, Piini achieved excellent photographic results using his custom-modified telescope system. The observation included clear views of Baily's Beads, the Diamond Ring, the corona, and several planets, accompanied by a noticeable temperature drop.

articles.title: Eclipse, from p. 3
articles.summary: The author, initially hesitant to write another book about an eclipse trip, was convinced to do so after receiving positive feedback on a previous publication. Despite considering a TV show instead, the encouragement led to the decision to write a new book, with the help of personal editors, for release later this year.

articles.title: Caribbean Eclipse '98 Terry Kahl
articles.summary: Terry Kahl recounts a 1998 Caribbean cruise on the Stella Solaris, dedicated to observing a total solar eclipse. The trip, coordinated by Ted Pedas, featured astronomy enrichment programs, expert lecturers, and optimal positioning arranged by a meteorologist, leading to a spectacular viewing experience. Beyond the eclipse, the cruise offered opportunities for stargazing and celebrations.

articles.title: SUBMIT
articles.summary: This document is an announcement encouraging members to submit articles for publication in the *SIAA Ephemeris* newsletter. Submissions should be sent to Dave North via email by the tenth of the month to be included in the following month's issue, and must include the author's name and phone number.

articles.title: Lunar David North
articles.summary: David North is presenting a "How To Observe The Moon" session for a Beginning Astronomy Class on May 2nd, coinciding with Astronomy Day. The article provides practical lunar observation tips for May 1998, detailing specific craters and features best viewed during the first quarter, eastern libration, and southern libration, including advice for Apollo 11 enthusiasts.

articles.title: On "The" Supernova:
articles.summary: The author recounts a personal observation of supernova SN1998S in galaxy NGC 3877, marveling at the immense energy released during a star's final collapse. The article provides clear instructions for locating NGC 3877 via star hop from Chi Ursa Majoris and assures that SN1998S is easily visible even with smaller telescopes, encouraging others to observe the celestial event.

articles.title: On New Telescopes:
articles.summary: The author expresses delight regarding the emergence of numerous new telescopes in the amateur astronomy market, finding the fresh topics refreshing for discussion. While noting past debates about brands like Meades and Tascos, the author states a personal indifference to the place-of-origin for these new units.

articles.title: On Observing The Deep Sky:
articles.summary: The article highlights Mallas, a skilled deep-sky observer, who consistently used increased magnification to discern fine detail in celestial objects, even with small instruments. The author confirms that such detail is achievable with modest apertures and emphasizes Mallas's work as an encouragement for beginners to develop their observational skills.

articles.title: On Moving-Mirror Focus:
articles.summary: This article discusses the utility of a moving primary mirror in a telescope, which allows for adjusting the focal plane's location. This feature is crucial for accommodating various telescope accessories, particularly cameras, that have different backfocus requirements. It prevents the common frustration of being unable to achieve focus when attaching diverse equipment.

articles.title: On April 1:
articles.summary: On April 1, 1998, an amateur astronomer claimed to have visually detected the 2.7 Kelvin cosmic microwave background radiation from Fremont Peak State Park. The observer detailed peculiar preparation methods, including four hours of dark adaptation with a mask, consuming bilberry jam, and using a homemade collimator, alluding to the observation being an April Fool's joke.

articles.title: PERIODICAL PUBLICATION STATEMENT
articles.summary: This document is a formal publication statement for the "SJAA Ephemeris," the monthly newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association. It specifies that the newsletter is published 12 times a year, from January through December, and provides the association's mailing address.

articles.title: EDITOR'S EXTRAS
articles.summary: This editor's update highlights upcoming events, including a May 9 meeting featuring John Dobson, and reports on the successful April 4 swap meet and auction which raised over $573, plus $84 for the eyepiece fund. Significant progress is reported on Fremont Peak Observatory repairs, with a $5000 donation received from SJAA, allowing for new roofing and siding, though the 30" telescope's opening day is pushed to late-May. Additionally, Akkana Peck has taken over the 'Shallow Sky' column, while David North will cover 'Lunacy' (Moon duties) and lead a Beginning Astronomy class on the Moon.

articles.title: To Subscribe to/Unsubscribe from the SJAA Mailing List send mail to
articles.summary: This document provides instructions on how to subscribe to or unsubscribe from the SJAA (San Jose Astronomical Association) mailing list. Users need to send an email to sjaa-request@seds.org with a blank subject line and either 'subscribe' or 'unsubscribe' in the body. The information is noted to be from the SJAA Ephemeris, May 1998 issue.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: This article, titled "COMET COMMENTS" by Don Machholz, reports on several comet-related updates, including new discoveries by the SOHO satellite and during an asteroid search, details about Comet C/1998 G1 (Linear) and Comet Tempel-Tuttle's nucleus. It notes generally low comet activity, mentioning Comet Hale-Bopp and Comet Meunier-Dupouy, and highlights SOHO's significant role as the most active comet discoverer, primarily finding short-lived sungrazers.

articles.title: Ephemerides (for 0h UT)
articles.summary: This article provides ephemerides for two comets, C/1997 J2 (Meunier-Dupouy) and C/1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp), detailing their Right Ascension, Declination, magnitude, and elevation for dates between early May and early June, calculated for 0h UT. It also lists significant orbital elements for both comets, such as perihelion date and distance, inclination, and eccentricity. Contact information for Don Machholz is included.

articles.title: BOARD MEETING NOTES
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) board of directors held its March 1998 meeting, during which new officers were elected, including Ed Erbeck as President and Dave North as Vice President. Key decisions included approving the previous meeting's minutes, confirming John Dobson as the May general meeting speaker, and unanimously voting to donate $5000 from the observatory fund to FPOA for observatory damage repair.

articles.title: Lunar
articles.summary: This document presents a calendar of the main lunar phases for a given month, detailing the exact time and date for the First Quarter, Full Moon, Last Quarter, and New Moon. It also provides the corresponding rise, transit, and set times for each phase, all specified in Pacific Daylight Time (PDT).

articles.title: Mercury
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for the planet Mercury, detailing its astronomical data for specific dates. It includes its magnitude, distance (A.U.), rise, transit, and set times, as well as its Right Ascension (R.A.) and Declination (Dec.) for the 7th, 17th, and 27th of an unspecified month.

articles.title: Venus
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for the planet Venus, listing its astronomical position and visibility data for three specific dates. It includes the planet's distance in Astronomical Units, visual magnitude, rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination.

articles.title: Mars
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for Mars, detailing its magnitude, distance (2.49 A.U.), and key observational data for three specific dates. It includes rise, transit, and set times, along with its celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) for those dates.

articles.title: Jupiter
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for Jupiter, detailing its apparent magnitude, distance from the Sun, and daily rise, transit, and set times. It also lists Jupiter's right ascension and declination for three specific dates (07, 17, 27), offering essential data for observers.

articles.title: Saturn
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for the planet Saturn, detailing its position and visibility over a period. It includes rise, transit, and set times, along with right ascension and declination for three specific dates. Additionally, it lists Saturn's approximate distance in A.U. and its apparent magnitude.

articles.title: SOL Star Type G2V Intelligent Life in System?
articles.summary: This article presents a table of astronomical data, likely an ephemeris for an object within a G2V star system (implied to be our Sun, 'SOL'). It lists rise, transit, and set times, along with Right Ascension and Declination for several dates. The title poses a question about intelligent life within such a system.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight
articles.summary: This document presents a schedule for astronomical twilight, detailing the specific begin and end times for several Julian Dates. It provides practical data for understanding when the sky is sufficiently dark for astronomical observations.

articles.title: Siderealtime
articles.summary: This document provides a tabular representation of sidereal time, specifically showing the transit Right Ascension at local midnight for three different dates: the 7th, 17th, and 27th of a month. The data illustrates a progression in sidereal time (or a related value) over these dates. This appears to be a reference table for astronomical calculations.

articles.title: Darkest Saturday Night
articles.summary: The article, titled "Darkest Saturday Night," provides astronomical timing details for May 23, 1998. It lists the times for sunset, the end of astronomical twilight, moonset, and the beginning of dawn, indicating the period of optimal darkness for sky observation. This information helps in planning stargazing activities for that specific night.

articles.title: Activities Through Other Clubs
articles.summary: This article outlines various astronomical observing activities offered by different clubs. TAC provides indefinite Wednesday observing at the Montebello site and hosts mobile first-quarter and Van Meter third-quarter Friday star parties, all requiring checking their website for details. PAS opens Foothill Observatory for public viewing on clear Friday evenings and conducts solar viewing on clear Saturday mornings, encouraging SJAA members to attend these programs.

articles.title: May
articles.summary: This document outlines key events for the month of May, including a Solar Program and evening observation on Astronomy Day (May 2nd). It also lists the PAS General Meeting on May 8th, featuring a presentation on Helioseismology from SOHO, and the PAS Board Meeting on May 13th, both held at Foothill College.

articles.title: June
articles.summary: This document outlines the schedule for the Peninsula Astronomical Society (PAS) in June. It announces a PAS General Meeting on June 12th at Foothill College, featuring a discussion on the 'Apollo 13 Accident,' and a PAS Board Meeting on June 17th at the Foothill College Observatory.

articles.title: DIRECTIONS TO SJAA PLACES
articles.summary: This document provides detailed driving directions to three locations frequented by the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA): Houge Park, Henry Coe State Park, and Fremont Peak State Park. It offers specific turn-by-turn instructions from major highways to each site, noting geographical context and any applicable entrance fees.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and members of the Board of Directors for an unspecified organization. It provides the names and contact phone numbers for the President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer, and several Directors.

articles.title: Ephemeris Staff
articles.summary: This document lists the staff members for 'Ephemeris', detailing key roles such as Editor, Circulation, Layout, and Proofing. It includes the names of the individuals in each position along with their respective contact numbers.

articles.title: Mike Koop
articles.summary: This document outlines the status of a telescope loan program, likely for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), managed by Mike Koop. It details current and extended scope loans, lists telescopes available for immediate borrowing, and provides a waiting list for popular instruments. The article also includes contact information for Mike Koop and specific notes regarding scope repairs or loan extensions.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) membership form, detailing options for new or renewal memberships at a cost of $15 for regular and $5 for junior members. It also provides an option to add a Sky & Telescope subscription for an additional $27. Instructions for payment by check and submission, either in person at a meeting or by mail to the treasurer, are included.
